newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS - Buba presses attack on revaluation scheme.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Buba presses attack on revaluation scheme.

text.p: The Bundesbank on Monday pressed home its attack on the government's plan to revalue the central bank's official reserves, with one council member saying the future of the euro was entering a crucial stage.

Speaking at a reception hosted by a state central bank, Bundesbank council member Edgar Meister said the monetary union project may enter "rougher waters" in the weeks and months ahead and warned that Germany must not lose its role as guardian of monetary stability.

Meister added the French election outcome on Sunday, which saw the Socialist-led left win a resounding victory, had changed the environment for Europe's planned monetary union and said it may become clear in the next few weeks whether the euro will be a stable currency.
"Since yesterday the constellation has been altered so that we might know in the next few weeks, not in 1998, whether the euro will be a stable currency," Meister said.

"Germany must not allow its role as guardian of stability to be torn out of its hands," Meister said. "If the euro were to be a soft currency it would not have sufficient acceptance in the population," he said.

Speaking at the same event, Bundesbank vice president Johann Wilhelm Gaddum said there had been no change in the Bundesbank's position on Bonn's attempt to revalue the central bank's official reserves. "The position that the Bundesbank had taken after its meeting on Wednesday describes the position of the Bundesbank and nothing has changed about that," he said in answer to a question.

After a council meeting last Wednesday, the Bundesbank issued a statement rejecting the government's plan to revalue its official reserves at higher levels and transfer some of the proceeds to Bonn to reduce its Budget deficit.
The Bundesbank said the plan would undermine the central bank's independence and ran the risk of threatening the stability of the euro.
Gaddum added the statement included elements of potential compromise, but was also very clear in its position in confronting the government's plan.
He said it was now up to the parliament to decide the outcome of the revaluation debate, but declined to say what that outcome might be, saying "its too early to say."
The Bundesbank's reluctance to sign on to Bonn's revaluation scheme, meanwhile, won the support of a prominent government economic advisor.

Horst Siebert, president of the Kiel Institute fuer Weltwirtschaft (IFW), one of Germany's leading economic institutes, told the Handelsblatt newspaper that he agreed with the Bundesbank that forcing through the revaluation would hurt its independence.
This could also hurt the European Central Bank as the Bundesbank was a particular role model for the future European monetary policy-making group, he said.
Chancellor Helmut Kohl's ruling coalition vowed, however, to push on with its controversial plan to revalue Bundesbank reserves after government leaders held a crisis meeting on budget woes in Bonn.
"On the question of the revaluation, we are still unified in the belief that this is right," Chancellery Minister Friedrich Bohl told journalists outside Kohl's office after the four-hour meeting.
